anselm: Anselm of Canterbury (1033-1109), a medieval Benedictine monk and Archbishop of Canterbury, is famous for the ontological argument: the claim that God's existence follows from the very concept of a being 'than which nothing greater can be conceived'. He also wrote influentially on why God became human, divine foreknowledge, and how guilt, punishment, and forgiveness fit together.
beauvoir: Simone de Beauvoir (1908-1986), French existentialist philosopher and novelist, is a founder of modern feminism. In The Second Sex she argued that woman is constructed as 'the Other' and that 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' - an early account of gender as socially made rather than given.
chalmers: David Chalmers (b. 1966), Australian-born philosopher now working in New York, is best known for formulating the 'hard problem of consciousness' - why physical processes give rise to subjective experience at all - and for the 'philosophical zombie' thought experiment. He also defends the extended mind and takes simulation scenarios seriously as metaphysical hypotheses.
clark: Andy Clark (b. 1957), a British philosopher of mind, is a leading proponent of the extended mind thesis: the idea that notebooks, smartphones, and other tools can literally count as parts of our thinking. His work on embodiment and predictive processing blurs the boundary between brain, body, and world.
dewey: John Dewey (1859-1952), American pragmatist and perhaps the most influential philosopher the United States has produced, treated philosophy as a tool for solving real problems rather than a system of eternal truths. He argued that democracy is a way of life, not just a voting mechanism, and reshaped education around learning by doing and reflective experience.
foucault: Michel Foucault (1926-1984), French philosopher and historian, studied how power operates through knowledge, institutions, and everyday practices rather than only through laws and rulers. His books on prisons, clinics, and sexuality introduced ideas like discipline, docile bodies, and surveillance, showing how modern societies shape people from the inside.
frankfurt: Harry Frankfurt (1929-2023), American moral philosopher long at Princeton, is known for two very different ideas. His account of second-order desires - wanting to want things - grounded an influential theory of personhood and free will, while his slim essay 'On Bullshit' defined bullshit as speech produced with no concern for the truth.
frankl: Viktor Frankl (1905-1997), Austrian psychiatrist and Holocaust survivor, founded logotherapy, a school of therapy centered on meaning. In Man's Search for Meaning, drawing on his time in the concentration camps, he argued that the deepest human drive is the search for meaning, which can be sustained even in terrible suffering - a stance often read alongside existentialism.
heraclitus: Heraclitus (c. 535-475 BC), a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from Ephesus, is famous for the doctrine that everything flows: reality is constant change, like a river you cannot step into twice. He held that this flux is governed by logos, a rational ordering principle, and that opposites depend on and transform into one another.
hobbes: Thomas Hobbes (1588-1679), English philosopher and one of the founders of social contract theory, argued in Leviathan that without a sovereign power, life in the state of nature would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. Rational, self-interested individuals therefore agree to authorize an absolute state in exchange for peace and security.
kuhn: Thomas Kuhn (1922-1996), American physicist turned historian and philosopher of science, argued in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions that science does not grow by steady accumulation of facts but through paradigm shifts, in which an entire framework of theory and practice is replaced. The book made 'paradigm' part of everyday speech.
leopold: Aldo Leopold (1887-1948), American forester, ecologist, and writer, is a founder of environmental ethics. In A Sand County Almanac he proposed the land ethic, extending moral consideration beyond individuals to the whole biotic community of soils, waters, plants, and animals, so that land is treated as a member of the community rather than a commodity.
lewis: David Lewis (1941-2001), American-born philosopher long at Princeton, is widely regarded as one of the most systematically inventive metaphysicians of the twentieth century. His modal realism - the controversial thesis that possible worlds are as real as our own - underpins his influential work on causation, time travel, free will, and personal identity.
machiavelli: Niccolo Machiavelli (1469-1527), Florentine diplomat and political writer, is often called the founder of modern political science. In The Prince he broke with classical and Christian moralizing, arguing that rulers must learn how 'not to be good' when necessity demands, and analyzing power through virtu (skill and strength of will) and fortuna (luck).
melanie-klein: Melanie Klein (1882-1960), Austrian-born British psychoanalyst, pioneered psychoanalysis of young children and founded object relations theory. Building on Freud, she emphasized earliest infancy, unconscious fantasy, and the death drive, arguing that envy, guilt, and the capacity for reparation shape the psyche from the start.
merleau-ponty: Maurice Merleau-Ponty (1908-1961), French phenomenologist, made the lived body central to philosophy. Against both Cartesian dualism and pure intellectualism, he argued that we perceive and act through embodied engagement with the world: the body is not a machine the mind drives but our very way of having a world.
roland-barthes: Roland Barthes (1915-1980), French literary theorist and essayist, was a major figure in structuralism and semiotics - the study of how signs carry meaning. He is best known for 'The Death of the Author', the claim that a text's meaning is made by readers and cultural codes rather than fixed by the writer's intention.
schopenhauer: Arthur Schopenhauer (1788-1860), German philosopher who began as a follower of Kant, is philosophy's great pessimist. He held that the world at bottom is Will - a blind, restless striving - so life oscillates between suffering and boredom, and that aesthetic contemplation, compassion, and ascetic denial offer the only temporary release.
sidgwick: Henry Sidgwick (1838-1900), Victorian English philosopher, gave utilitarianism its most rigorous classical statement in The Methods of Ethics, wrestling honestly with the conflict between self-interest and the greatest-happiness principle. He also helped found the analytical style of ethics still used today.
singer: Peter Singer (b. 1946), Australian philosopher, is among the most influential living applied ethicists. His Animal Liberation (1975) introduced 'speciesism' - prejudice in favor of one's own species - and his drowning child argument holds that affluence carries strong obligations to aid distant strangers, both flowing from his utilitarianism.
sun-tzu: Sun Tzu, Chinese military strategist traditionally placed in the fifth century BC and credited with The Art of War, taught that the highest victory is won without fighting - through deception, positioning, and knowing both oneself and the enemy. His maxim 'know your enemy' has made him a touchstone far beyond warfare.
wollstonecraft: Mary Wollstonecraft (1759-1797), English writer and philosopher, is a founder of feminist philosophy. In A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) she argued that women appear inferior only because they are denied education and the chance to cultivate their reason - differences of circumstance and training, not of nature.
young: Iris Marion Young (1949-2006), American political philosopher, was a leading feminist and justice theorist. Her 'Five Faces of Oppression' mapped how exploitation, marginalization, powerlessness, cultural imperialism, and violence work as structures, and she argued that justice requires not just fair distribution but transforming oppressive institutions.
zeno-citium: Zeno of Citium (c. 334-262 BC), a Phoenician-born former merchant who taught in Athens after being shipwrecked, founded Stoicism. He taught that virtue is the only true good and that we should live in accord with nature and reason - ideas his successors developed into the dichotomy of control and Stoic tranquility.
